a: An oracle
p: Zechariah 9-14 has two oracles with this heading: 9:1 and 12:1.
b: Massa' comes from nasa', 'lift up,' so it can mean 'a load' or 'a lifting of the voice.' The King James Version prints 'burden.' This Plain keeps 'oracle,' the site's word for it (Isaiah 13:1; Proverbs 30:1). The same heading opens Zechariah 12:1 and Malachi 1:1, and many scholars think the three headings mark three units added at the end of the Book of the Twelve (see the book page). Jeremiah 23:33-40 plays on both senses of the word. Unlike Zechariah 1:1, 7 and 7:1, this part of the book gives no date.

a: Hadrach
t: Hadrach, in the north of Syria
p: Hadrach (Akkadian Hatarikka) was a city and small kingdom near Hamath.
b: Hadrach is named once in the Bible. It is the Hatarikka of Assyrian records, a city-state in the north of Syria near Hamath, and the Aramaic stele of King Zakkur of Hamath (about 800 BC) calls it Hazrak. Assyrian kings fought there in the 700s BC, and Tiglath-pileser III took it into his empire. So the oracle begins at the far north, in the old Aramean lands, and then moves down the coast to Philistia. The Greek translators did not know the name and wrote 'Sedrach' (Swete's text). Sifre Deuteronomy (Pisqa 1) records a rabbinic wordplay by R. Judah: Hadrach is chad 'sharp' and rakh 'tender,' the Messiah who is harsh to the nations and tender to Israel; R. Yose ben Dormasqit answers with a different reading. That is a later midrashic reading, not the plain sense.

a: and Damascus is where it settles
p: Alexander's march in 332 BC is one view; an Assyrian date and a Persian date are others.
b: The list runs from north to south: Hadrach, Damascus, Hamath, Tyre, Sidon, then Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron and Ashdod. (1) Alexander the Great, 333-332 BC. After the battle of Issus he took Damascus, Sidon came over to him, Tyre fell after a siege of seven months, and Gaza was stormed. Many who date these chapters in the Greek period use this (see 9:13). (2) The 8th century BC, the time of Tiglath-pileser III, who took the same lands; older critics who thought chapters 9-14 came from before the exile held this. (3) The Persian period, when the Phoenician and Philistine cities were Persian subjects, and the prophet of chapters 1-8 could have spoken. The Plain does not choose. The book page sets out the arguments about the unity and date of chapters 9-14.

a: Every human eye, and every tribe of Israel, looks to the LORD
p: The Hebrew allows two readings: people look to the LORD, or the LORD watches people.
b: The Hebrew is 'for to the LORD is the eye of humankind and of all the tribes of Israel.' Read one way, all people, not only Israel, look to the LORD in the crisis the oracle describes (so the Plain). Read the other way, the LORD has his eye on humankind and on Israel's tribes, as the Septuagint takes it (Swete's text has 'the LORD looks on people and all the tribes of Israel'). The word 'humankind' ('adam) beside Israel hints that the nations are in view, as in 9:7 and 9:10.

a: Tyre built herself a fortress
p: Tyre (Hebrew Tsor) and 'fortress' (matsor) sound alike; the city stood on an island.
b: The Hebrew puns on the city's name: Tsor built matsor. Island Tyre was a trading power: Ezekiel 27 lists its wares, and Ezekiel 28:4-5 says it gathered gold and silver by its wisdom, the same two metals and the same word 'wise' that appear here (9:2-3). Nebuchadnezzar besieged the city for years (Ezekiel 26:7-14; 29:17-20). In 332 BC Alexander built a causeway from the mainland to the island and took the city (Arrian, Anabasis, book 2). Verse 4 says the Lord will 'batter her strength in the sea,' which suits an island; the Hebrew word chel can be strength, wealth or wall.
r: Isaiah 23:1-18; Ezekiel 26:1-21; Ezekiel 27:1-36; Ezekiel 28:1-10; Joel 3:4-8; Amos 1:9-10

a: Ashkelon will watch and be terrified
p: Gath is missing from the list, as in Amos 1:6-8; the king of Gaza perishes.
b: Four of the five Philistine cities are named: Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron and Ashdod. Gath is left out, as in Amos 1:6-8 and Jeremiah 25:20, and was probably ruined by this time (2 Kings 12:17; Amos 6:2). On the Alexander view, Gaza held out under its commander Batis, a eunuch, until Alexander took it (Arrian, Anabasis 2.25-27). On an earlier view the verse recalls Assyrian conquests of the 8th and 7th centuries BC. A king of Gaza fits both, since Gaza had kings in the Assyrian and the Persian periods.

a: A mixed people
p: The rare Hebrew word mamzer names someone of unclear or forbidden birth.
b: Mamzer appears only here and in Deuteronomy 23:2, where it names a person born of a forbidden union who may not join the assembly. Here it is read as 'a mixed population,' foreigners settled in the ruined city; as 'a bastard' (the King James Version); or as a scornful name for a people with no standing. The Septuagint has 'foreigners' (allogeneis). The sense is shame: the proud Philistines will be replaced by mixed settlers. Assyria had resettled conquered lands this way (2 Kings 17:24).

a: Those of them who remain will be kept for our God
p: A remnant of the Philistines will join Judah, as the Jebusites did.
b: After 'I will take their blood out of their mouths' (blood and meat from idol feasts, against Leviticus 17:10-14), the oracle turns: the survivors 'will be left over for our God,' a remnant, and will count among Judah's clans like a 'eleph (a clan, literally 'a thousand'; the Septuagint has chiliarchos, a chief of a thousand). Ekron 'like the Jebusites' recalls the old inhabitants of Jerusalem who were taken into David's city (2 Samuel 5:6-9; 24:18-25 on Araunah the Jebusite). Israel's old enemy becomes an insider. Christian readers have seen in this the nations joining God's people.

a: to stand guard
t: A guard, a post or a pillar?
p: The Hebrew word can be read as a guard post, a standing pillar, or 'against an army.'
b: The word is mitstsavah, 'a post, an outpost' (the related noun matstsav names the Philistine garrison in 1 Samuel 13:23; 14:1). Some read it with other vowels as matstsevah, 'a standing stone,' and others as mitstsava', 'from an army,' so that the LORD camps at his house to guard it. The Septuagint has 'a stand' (anastema). The picture is the LORD himself camping around the Temple so that no army can pass (compare Psalm 34:7; Isaiah 31:5; 2 Kings 6:17). The verse ends with his own sight, as in Exodus 3:7: 'now I have seen.'

a: Be very glad, Daughter Zion
t: Rejoice: the city told to shout
p: The call echoes Zephaniah 3:14 and Isaiah 62:11.
b: 'Daughter Zion' is the personified city (the site's rendering). The cry matches Zephaniah 3:14, "Daughter Zion, give a ringing cry" (Zephaniah 3:14), where too the reason for joy is the LORD, the king, in her midst. Isaiah 62:11 speaks to Daughter Zion as well: the LORD's salvation is coming. Matthew 21:5 blends the two prophets: 'Tell the daughter of Zion' comes from Isaiah, and the rest follows Zechariah. John 12:15 begins 'Daughter of Zion, have no fear,' which echoes Zephaniah 3:16 and Isaiah 40:9. Neither Gospel quotes 'be very glad' at all.

a: He is righteous, and he has been rescued
p: The Hebrew says the king 'has been saved'; 'victorious' is a guess at the sense.
b: Nosha' is a passive form (Niphal) of the verb 'to save': the king is 'saved' or 'delivered,' that is, rescued or vindicated by God. It is not 'saving,' as the Septuagint's sozon has it ('righteous and saving'), and it does not say 'victorious.' Three ideas lie behind the word: the king is delivered by God (compare Deuteronomy 33:29, Israel as a people saved by the LORD); he is vindicated, like the righteous sufferer of the psalms; or he is the one through whom God saves. Matthew and John do not quote this phrase. The Plain keeps the passive. 'Righteous' (tsaddiq) is the king who rules by God's justice (Jeremiah 23:5).

a: He is poor
p: The word means poor and afflicted; Matthew's Greek 'gentle' is a different choice.
b: 'Ani means 'poor, afflicted, bowed down' and is the word for the lowly who depend on God (Zephaniah 3:12, 'afflicted and poor'; Psalm 40:17). Many English Bibles write 'humble' or 'lowly,' which moves the word from a person's place in society to his character. The Septuagint has praus, 'gentle,' and Matthew 21:5 follows it ('He is gentle'). The same Hebrew word names 'the poor of the flock' in 11:7 and 11:11: a poor king and a poor flock, and the book links them. A poor king is also the opposite of the chariot-driving kings that verse 10 removes.

a: on a donkey, on a young male donkey, the foal of a she-donkey
t: The king on a donkey and the Gospels
p: One animal in Hebrew; Matthew has two, Mark, Luke and John one.
b: The Hebrew gives one animal in two phrases: 'a donkey, that is, a young male donkey, the foal of female donkeys' (the second line sharpens the first, as Hebrew poetry does). The donkey was a ruler's mount before horses and chariots: Judges 5:10; 10:4; 12:14; Solomon rode David's mule to be anointed (1 Kings 1:33, 38); Genesis 49:10-11 pictures the ruler of Judah tying his donkey to the vine. Matthew 21:2, 7 has two animals, 'a donkey tied up, and a colt with her,' and puts Jesus on 'them.' Mark 11:2 and Luke 19:30 have only a colt, and John 12:14 'a little donkey.' Matthew quotes it as "on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a work animal" (Matthew 21:5). All the Gospel citations leave out 'righteous and rescued.' See the card on the entry.
r: Genesis 49:10-11; Judges 5:10; 1 Kings 1:33; Matthew 21:2-7; Mark 11:2; Luke 19:30; John 12:14-15

a: I will take the chariot away from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem
p: The king of peace removes war horses from both Ephraim and Jerusalem.
b: Israel's kings were told not to gather horses or send to Egypt for them (Deuteronomy 17:16), yet Solomon did (1 Kings 10:26-29), and the prophets called horses and chariots a false trust (Isaiah 31:1; Hosea 1:7; Micah 5:10). The oracle names 'Ephraim' (the north) beside Jerusalem: the divided kingdom is under one king. The speaker moves from 'I' (the LORD) to 'he' (the king) and back with no break, which is common in Hebrew poetry. The bow is the last weapon named. In 9:13 the LORD will bend Judah like a bow, so peace is won by a fight.
r: Deuteronomy 17:16; Hosea 1:7; Micah 5:10; Isaiah 31:1; Psalm 46:9; Zechariah 9:13

a: from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth
p: The same words as Psalm 72:8.
b: These are the same Hebrew words as Psalm 72:8, a prayer for the king: "from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth" (Psalm 72:8). 'The River' is the Euphrates, the old northern limit of David's rule (Genesis 15:18), and 'the ends of the earth' goes far beyond it. Micah 5:4 uses the second phrase of the ruler from Bethlehem. So the coming king is given the reach of the royal psalm. 'Sea to sea' is read as the Mediterranean to the Dead Sea or the Persian Gulf, or as all the waters of the world.

a: because of the blood of your covenant
p: It recalls Sinai (Exodus 24:8); 'your' is feminine, so the city is addressed.
b: 'The blood of your covenant' goes back to Exodus 24:8, where Moses splashed blood on the people: "Here is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has cut with you" (Exodus 24:8). The 'your' is feminine singular, so the speaker still addresses Zion (as in 9:9). The covenant sealed at Sinai is the ground on which God frees the prisoners. Christians hear in it the words of Jesus at the last supper (Matthew 26:28; Mark 14:24). That is a later use. The Hebrew says nothing of a new covenant; for that see Jeremiah 31:31-34.

a: a pit with no water in it
p: A cistern or dungeon: a prison, or a picture of exile.
b: A pit without water is an emptied cistern used as a prison: Joseph (Genesis 37:24) and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 38:6) were put in one. It stands for exile and helplessness (Psalm 40:2; Isaiah 24:22). Isaiah 42:7 and 61:1 use the same prison language for the exiles' freedom. Some Christian writers read the pit as the world of the dead and the prisoners as those Christ set free on Holy Saturday (the 'harrowing of hell'). That goes beyond the Hebrew, which speaks of captives in exile.
orig: בּוֹר אֵין מַיִם בּוֹ (bor 'en mayim bo)
r: Genesis 37:24; Jeremiah 38:6; Psalm 40:2; Isaiah 24:22; Isaiah 42:7; Isaiah 61:1

a: prisoners of hope
p: A rare word for 'fortress' (bitsaron), and 'double' as full repayment.
b: 'Prisoners of hope' means prisoners who still hope, or whose hope is in the LORD. Bitsaron, 'fortress,' is found only here; the Septuagint has 'strongholds.' 'I will give back double' echoes Isaiah 40:2 (Jerusalem has received double for her sins) and Isaiah 61:7 (double in place of shame); in the law the firstborn took a double share (Deuteronomy 21:17), and Job got back twice what he lost (Job 42:10). Here 'double' means full restoration. The Hebrew maggid mishneh can also be read 'declaring a second time.' The Plain keeps 'double.'

a: your sons, Greece
p: Yavan (Greece, Ionia) leads many scholars to a Greek-period date.
b: Yavan is Ionia, the Greeks. In Genesis 10:2, 4 Javan is a son of Japheth; Ezekiel 27:13, 19 lists Javan among Tyre's traders; Joel 3:6 and Daniel 8:21; 10:20; 11:2 name Greece, the last as a kingdom. Many critical scholars date 9:1-17 after Alexander (332 BC), so that 'Zion's sons against Greece's sons' reflects the wars against the Seleucids (1 Maccabees). Others hold that Greek traders and soldiers were known in Israel's world from the 8th century BC, and in the Persian wars (Marathon, 490 BC; Salamis, 480 BC) Greece was the great western power, so a date in Zechariah's own time can speak of it. Later Jewish and Christian readers have often applied the verse to the Maccabees; that rests on the Greek-period date.
r: Genesis 10:2-4; Joel 3:6; Daniel 8:21; Daniel 11:2; 1 Maccabees 1:1; Isaiah 66:19

a: I have bent Judah like a bow for myself
t: Judah the bow, Ephraim the arrow
p: The LORD uses Judah as a bow and Ephraim as the arrow; then Zion as a sword.
b: The picture is of an archer bending a bow and fitting an arrow (the Hebrew 'filled' is the loading, as in 2 Kings 9:24, 'filled his hand with the bow'). The two halves of the nation are one weapon in the LORD's hand: Judah the bow, Ephraim the arrow, north and south joined after the split of 1 Kings 12 (as in 9:10 and 10:6). In the next verse the LORD's own arrow flashes. 'A warrior's sword' makes Zion a weapon he wields, not an army that wins alone. Commentators note the tension with 9:10, which ends war's weapons: here the peace comes by a battle.

a: walk in the gales from the south
t: The LORD comes as a storm warrior
p: Teman and Sinai: the LORD arrives from the south with lightning and a horn.
b: The LORD coming from the south in a storm belongs to the oldest poetry: Deuteronomy 33:2 (from Sinai, from Seir), Judges 5:4-5 (from Seir and Edom), Habakkuk 3:3-4 (God from Teman, with lightning at his side), Psalm 18:7-15. The 'storm winds of the south' (se'arot teman) are gales out of the desert. The ram's horn (shofar) is the signal of war and of the LORD's coming, as at Sinai (Exodus 19:16). Verse 15 then shows the LORD of Armies as the people's shield.

a: like the sprinkling bowl, like the corners of the altar
t: Drunk and full: a hard verse
p: A bowl for splashing blood, and the altar corners where blood was thrown.
b: The Hebrew is hard and no translation is certain. 'They will eat, and they will crush the sling stones' can be 'they will devour and trample sling stones' (the stones the enemy slung), or a figure for the enemy. 'They will drink and roar as if from wine' describes a victory feast. The mizraq is a sprinkling bowl for catching the blood from sacrifices, which was thrown against the altar (Exodus 27:3; Leviticus 1:5; Numbers 7:84). The image is of warriors as full as that bowl. The Septuagint has 'they will drink them like wine,' and the Hebrew lines that follow are read differently in the old versions.

a: stones from a crown, flashing above his land
p: The people are jewels in the LORD's crown; 'flashing' may also mean 'lifted like a banner.'
b: The verb mitnosesot is found only here. It may come from nus, 'to sparkle,' or from nes, 'a banner,' so the jewels are 'lifted high.' The Septuagint has 'holy stones rolling on his land.' The LORD's flock (the shepherd picture, 'like a flock') becomes a royal crown. Isaiah 62:3 has the same turn: the people are a crown of beauty in the LORD's hand. The mixed figures, flock and jewels, are typical of the chapter's quick changes.

a: when the late rains are due
t: The spring rain, and who gives it
p: The late rains (March-April) ripened the grain; the LORD, not Baal, sends them.
b: Israel had two rainy seasons, the early rain of autumn and the 'spring' or late rain of March and April that filled the grain before harvest (Deuteronomy 11:14; Jeremiah 5:24; Joel 2:23). A late rain failing meant a lost crop. To ask the LORD for it is a pointed word, since Canaanite religion gave the storm and rain to Baal (see the 'teraphim' and diviners of 10:2, and Hosea 2:8-9 and 1 Kings 17-18). The Hebrew for 'storm clouds' (chazizim) is rare; Job 28:26; 38:25 uses it for lightning flashes. The verse moves from rain to a flock without a shepherd, because both are about whom Israel asks.

a: teraphim
p: Household images used to learn the future; the Plain keeps the Hebrew word.
b: The Plain keeps teraphim (as at Hosea 3:4), small household images used to ask for guidance: Rachel took her father's (Genesis 31:19, where the site's Plain says 'household gods'), Micah had them in his shrine (Judges 17:5), and Ezekiel 21:21 has Babylon's king consult them. Samuel linked them to rebellion (1 Samuel 15:23), and Josiah removed them (2 Kings 23:24). In Zechariah the teraphim 'speak harm' ('aven, which also means 'nothing'), dreamers give false comfort, and the people wander because they have no shepherd. The charge is the old one: asking an image what only the LORD can say.
r: Genesis 31:19; Judges 17:5; 1 Samuel 15:23; 2 Kings 23:24; Ezekiel 21:21; Hosea 3:4

a: they have no shepherd
p: In the ancient world a king was a shepherd; a people with a bad ruler was a flock with none.
b: From Egypt and Mesopotamia on, kings were called shepherds. A flock without one was a people scattered by defeat or neglect: Moses asks for a leader so the community will not be 'like sheep with no one to shepherd them' (Numbers 27:17); Micaiah saw Israel 'like a flock with no shepherd' (1 Kings 22:17); Ezekiel 34:5 says they were scattered 'for lack of a shepherd.' Zechariah 10-11 and 13:7 turn on the image, and Matthew 9:36 uses it of the crowds around Jesus: 'like sheep that have no shepherd.' See the shepherd topic.
r: Numbers 27:17; 1 Kings 22:17; Ezekiel 34:5; Matthew 9:36; John 10:11; Zechariah 11:4-17

a: the lead goats
p: A play on 'visit': the same Hebrew verb means 'call to account' and 'take care of.'
b: 'Attudim are male goats that lead a flock, and so leaders (Isaiah 14:9, 'the he-goats of the earth'; compare Ezekiel 34:17). The verb paqad, 'visit,' means to pay attention for good or for ill; the Hebrew uses it twice, 'I will call the lead goats to account' and 'the LORD of Armies will take care of his flock.' Jeremiah 23:2 has the same play against the shepherds who scattered the flock. The LORD's anger is at the shepherds, not at the sheep, and the sheep he cares for become a war horse.

a: From him come the cornerstone and the tent peg
p: The Hebrew does not say; the answers are Judah, the LORD or the new leader.
b: Four times the Hebrew says 'from him' (mimmennu): from him the pinnah, the tent peg, the war bow, the ruler. The word pinnah, 'corner,' also means a chief (Judges 20:2, 'pillars'; 1 Samuel 14:38, 'cornerstones of the people'), and a tent peg can be a steadying official (Isaiah 22:23). So these may be rulers who will come from Judah's house (the 'him' of 10:3). Another reading takes 'him' as the LORD, who is the true cornerstone (Isaiah 28:16) and peg and bow. Christian readers have taken it of Christ the cornerstone (Psalm 118:22; Isaiah 28:16 in the New Testament). The verse leaves 'him' open. The last word, noges, which the Plain renders 'ruler,' is the word for a taskmaster or oppressor (Exodus 3:7; Isaiah 9:4); here it is turned around, so that the oppressor's title is taken over by the rulers who come from Judah, or removed from Israel altogether. The Hebrew is hard, and the Plain keeps the neutral 'ruler.'

a: the house of Joseph
p: 'Joseph' (Ephraim) is the north, taken away by Assyria in 722 BC; they come home too.
b: 'The house of Joseph' is the northern kingdom (Ephraim and Manasseh, Joseph's sons), which Assyria carried away in 722-721 BC (2 Kings 17). Here Judah is strengthened and Joseph is saved: both halves of the people come home. The same hope is in Ezekiel 37:15-22 (two sticks made one), Jeremiah 31:1-9 and Hosea 11:10-11. Chapters 9-10 insist on the return of Ephraim (9:10, 13; 10:7), and Jewish and Christian readers later asked what happened to the 'lost tribes' (see the topic). The text says the LORD himself brings them, 'because I have compassion on them.'

a: I will bring them home
p: The Hebrew verb can come from shuv, 'return,' or yashav, 'settle.'
b: The form hoshavotim can be read from shuv ('I will bring them back') or from yashav ('I will make them live' or 'settle them'). The Septuagint has 'I will make them live' (katoikio). The Plain's 'bring them home' covers both senses. The verb shuv returns in 10:9 ('they will come back'), so a pun on the two roots is possible.

a: I will sow them among the peoples
p: God 'sows' Israel among the nations as seed, to grow where it falls.
b: Scattering is pictured as sowing. The verb for 'sow' (zara') is also the root of 'Jezreel,' 'God sows,' and Hosea turned it into a promise: 'I will sow her for myself in the land' (Hosea 2:23). Jeremiah 31:27 says the LORD will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with seed of people. Here the sowing among the peoples is the Dispersion, and in the far places the exiles remember the LORD, live with their children, and return. The line is a promise that exile is not the end of the seed.

a: from the land of Egypt and gather them from Assyria
t: Egypt and Assyria: the old powers as code
p: Egypt and Assyria stand for all the lands of the scattered.
b: By the time of this prophecy Assyria no longer ruled, and its name stands for the lands of the exile in general, with Egypt, where many Judeans had fled after 586 BC (Jeremiah 43-44). Isaiah 11:11 gives a longer list of the places the remnant will come from, 'from Assyria and Egypt, from Pathros and Cush.' Hosea 11:11 has the exiles trembling out of Egypt and Assyria like birds. The names were kept as a code for 'the great powers who took our people,' and Isaiah 19:23-25 reverses them: Egypt and Assyria will worship the LORD with Israel. 'Gilead and Lebanon' are the old territories of the north.

a: The Nile's deepest places will dry up.
p: The sea is struck and the river dries up, as at the Sea of Reeds.
b: The hero 'passes through the sea' and 'strikes down its waves,' and the Nile's depths dry up: the Exodus, told again (Exodus 14:21-22; 15:8-10), as Isaiah 11:15-16 and Isaiah 51:10 tell it. In Isaiah the new road dries a path home from Assyria and Egypt. In Zechariah the same powers are brought low (the 'pride of Assyria' and 'the scepter of Egypt'), and the returning flock crosses over. See the variant on 'the sea of distress.' Egypt's great river is called here ye'or, the Nile, the same word as in Exodus 7-8.

a: Open your doors, Lebanon
p: Lebanon's cedars are proud rulers, or the Temple, or the land in general.
b: The poem calls on Lebanon, Bashan and the Jordan thickets to wail because fire has felled them. Three readings. (1) Proud rulers. Cedars and oaks stand for the mighty (Isaiah 2:12-13; 10:33-34; Ezekiel 31), and the wailing shepherds of 11:3 are their rulers: a judgment on the leaders. (2) The Temple. Lebanon's cedar built the Temple and the royal 'House of the Forest of Lebanon' (1 Kings 5-7). The Babylonian Talmud says that forty years before the Temple's fall its doors opened by themselves, and Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai spoke to the Temple and quoted this verse (Yoma 39b); Josephus tells of a bronze gate that opened by itself before the Roman war (Jewish War 6.5.3). (3) The Land. The whole country is stripped. Christian writers have also taken it of the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70.

a: Shepherd the flock that is meant for killing
t: The shepherd who is paid and rejected
p: A sign act with two staffs: the prophet plays the shepherd of a flock that others will slaughter.
b: This is the strangest passage in the book. The LORD tells the prophet to be the shepherd of a doomed flock, and he does: he takes two staffs, removes three shepherds, asks for his pay and gets thirty shekels, throws the pay to the potter, and breaks both staffs. Then he is told to take a foolish shepherd's tools (11:15-17). It is a sign act like Jeremiah 13 and 19 or Ezekiel 4-5 and 37:15-22, but it is hard to tell what is acted and what is told. Proposals: (1) the prophet plays the part of the LORD, rejected shepherd of Israel (the commonest Christian reading, with Matthew 27:9-10); (2) he stands for a good ruler of the time, now unknown to us, rejected by the people; (3) it is a history of the leaders of Judah (the three shepherds, the breaking of the bond with Samaria) told as a parable; (4) the shepherd is a Jewish leader of the Greek period (some critical scholars). The base texts are Ezekiel 34 and Jeremiah 23:1-4.
r: Ezekiel 34:1-31; Jeremiah 23:1-4; Jeremiah 19:1-15; Ezekiel 37:15-22; Matthew 27:9-10; John 10:1-18

a: One I named Favor, and the other I named Union
p: Two staff names: pleasantness or favor, and bonds, ropes or union.
b: No'am is 'pleasantness, favor, grace' (Psalm 27:4, 'the beauty of the LORD'); the Septuagint writes Kallos, 'Beauty.' Hovelim is a plural of chevel, 'a rope, a cord, a measured plot, a bond, a pledge,' so the staff means 'Ropes,' 'Bonds,' or, since the staff's breaking cuts the 'brotherhood' (11:14), 'Union.' The Septuagint has Schoinisma, 'a measured share,' the allotted land. The first staff stands for the LORD's favor to the nations (the covenant of 11:10); the second for the bond between Judah and Israel. The Plain gives the sense it needs for the story and keeps the Hebrew in this note.

a: the three shepherds
p: More than forty answers have been given; the Hebrew says 'the three' as if known.
b: 'The three shepherds' has the article, so the first readers knew who was meant, but we do not. The answers run to dozens. Some choose three kings (for example the last kings of Judah), three offices (prophet, priest, king) or three foreign rulers. The Babylonian Talmud applies the verse to Moses, Aaron and Miriam, through whom Israel received the well, the pillar of cloud and the manna; when Miriam died the well disappeared, and when Moses died all the gifts disappeared (Taanit 9a). Many critical commentators decline to name them and call the verse an allusion to an event we cannot recover. 'In a single month' may be a number meaning 'quickly.' The Septuagint has the same 'three shepherds.'

a: the covenant I had cut with all the peoples
t: A covenant with all the peoples
p: The staff of Favor stands for a covenant that holds the nations back.
b: The covenant 'with all the peoples' (kol-ha'ammim) is nowhere else mentioned. Hosea 2:18 speaks of a covenant with wild animals that makes the land safe, and Job 5:23 of a covenant with the stones of the field. So some read the LORD's covenant with the nations as a promise that they would not harm his flock (the staff Favor); when it is broken, 11:6 follows and the neighbors crush the land. Others read 'peoples' as the tribes of Israel, as in Deuteronomy 33:3 and Genesis 28:3. The site's Plain says 'cut a covenant,' the Hebrew idiom for making one.

a: thirty shekels of silver
t: Thirty shekels: the price of a slave
p: In the law, thirty shekels was the compensation for a slave killed by an ox.
b: The price is an insult. Exodus 21:32 sets the compensation when an ox gores a slave to death: "silver, thirty shekels" (Exodus 21:32). The shepherd who had cared for the flock is paid what a worker is worth if a bull kills him. The Hebrew says only 'thirty of silver.' The Plain says 'shekels' because the pay was 'weighed out' (so also Jeremiah 32:9-10 for a field). Matthew 26:15 echoes the verse when the chief priests 'weighed out thirty silver coins' to Judas, and Matthew 27:3-10 completes the link (see 11:13). The Gospels give no motive for the amount; most readers see the deliberate Scripture echo.

a: that splendid price they put on me
p: The Hebrew word for 'splendid' (eder) is used for a price here with bitter irony.
b: Eder hayyeqar is literally 'the magnificence of the value.' The prophet repeats the word yaqar, 'valued, precious,' with biting scorn: 'the precious price at which I was valued by them.' The Septuagint changed the line completely: 'Put them in the furnace, and I will see if it is genuine, as it was tested for them.' Matthew 27:9 uses the Hebrew phrase's weight: 'the price of the one who was priced, the value some of Israel's sons put on him.' That doubled wording renders the double yaqar.

a: threw them in the LORD's house
p: Matthew blends Zechariah 11 with Jeremiah 18, 19 and 32 and names Jeremiah.
b: Matthew 27:3-10 tells how Judas threw the thirty silver coins into the sanctuary and the priests bought the Potter's Field with them. He writes: "Then the word spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled: 'And they took the thirty silver coins, the price of the one who was priced...'" (Matthew 27:9). The wording follows Zechariah 11:12-13, but the name is Jeremiah, who has a potter's house (Jeremiah 18:2-3), a potter's jar and a place of blood (Jeremiah 19:1-11) and a field bought with silver (Jeremiah 32:6-15). Explanations: (1) a mixed quotation named for the better-known prophet (the commonest view); (2) 'Jeremiah' names the whole scroll, which the Talmud lists first (Bava Batra 14b); (3) a mistake in the name (Calvin says he does not know how it came in; Augustine suggests a slip of Matthew's memory that God allowed, so that the prophets would be seen to speak with one spirit, Harmony of the Gospels 3.7); (4) Jerome reports a Hebrew apocryphon of Jeremiah, shown to him by a Nazarene, with these words in it, yet thinks the testimony more likely taken from Zechariah, since the evangelists and apostles gave the sense, not the exact words; (5) Joseph Mede held that these chapters were Jeremiah's (so the Calvin Translation Society's editor reports). See the card.
r: Matthew 27:3-10; Jeremiah 18:2-3; Jeremiah 19:1-13; Jeremiah 32:6-15; Acts 1:18-19; Zechariah 11:12

a: the brotherhood between Judah and Israel
p: A reversal of Ezekiel 37:15-22: the two sticks made one are here cut in two.
b: Ezekiel 37:15-22 joined two sticks, Judah's and Joseph's, into one in the prophet's hand as a promise of one nation. Zechariah breaks the staff of 'Union' and with it the 'brotherhood' (ha'achvah, found only here). Proposals for the event: the old split of Israel (1 Kings 12), a split in the early Persian period or later between Judah and the Samaritans (Samaria-Judah conflict in Nehemiah 4 and 6; Josephus tells of a Samaritan temple on Gerizim in Alexander's time), or a break inside Judah. The Septuagint reads 'the allotment between Judah and between Israel' (katochen). Chapters 9-10 had promised reunion; here it fails.

a: the tools of a foolish shepherd
p: A second sign act: the prophet plays the bad shepherd the LORD will let rule.
b: Now the prophet is to dress as the wrong kind of shepherd. 'Foolish' is 'evili, the stubborn fool of Proverbs. In 11:17 he is 'worthless' ('elil, the word that in the plural names idols, the 'worthless gods'), and a sword will cripple and blind him. The list in 11:16 turns Ezekiel 34:4 upside down (the shepherd who did not strengthen the weak or bandage the broken), and John 10:12 sets the hired man who leaves the sheep beside the good shepherd. Church fathers have often taken him as Antichrist; critical writers prefer a ruler or ruling class of the time. The LORD raises up this shepherd: that wording puts the judgment under his control.

a: who stretches out the heavens, lays the base of the earth, and forms the spirit of a human being inside him
p: Creation words open the oracle: heavens, earth and the human spirit.
b: This is the only place in the Bible where the LORD is said to 'form' (yatsar, the potter's verb) the spirit of a human being. The three-part praise matches Isaiah 42:5 (heavens, earth, breath and spirit), Isaiah 44:24 (stretching out the heavens, hammering out the earth), and Numbers 16:22 ('God of the spirits of all flesh'). The opening pictures the LORD as maker before he speaks of the war on Jerusalem. The spirit he formed in people he will pour out (12:10). The line also joins this oracle to the first, which began with the LORD's eye on humankind (9:1).
r: Isaiah 42:5; Isaiah 44:24; Numbers 16:22; Ecclesiastes 12:7; Genesis 2:7; Zechariah 12:10

a: makes all the peoples around her stagger
p: Jerusalem is the cup the nations drink and stagger from; the Greek has 'shaking thresholds.'
b: The Hebrew saf ra'al is 'a bowl of reeling.' The prophets spoke of a cup of the LORD's anger that nations drink to the dregs and fall (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15-29). Here the nations who attack Jerusalem drink from her. The Hebrew saf can also mean 'threshold,' and the Septuagint has 'shaking doorways' (prothyra saleuomena). Judah's part in the siege is unclear: 'it will be that way for Judah too' may mean that Judah too is besieged, or that Judah is forced to join the attack on Jerusalem (the 'tents of Judah' of 12:7 point to a split between countryside and city), or that Judah is in the siege against the invaders. The Plain keeps the Hebrew's open phrase.

a: a stone too heavy for any of the peoples
p: A test-of-strength stone: those who try to lift Jerusalem hurt themselves.
b: Jerome says that in his day every village in Palestine had large round stones that young men tried to lift to show their strength, and that 'a heavy stone' here means the same: those who try to lift Jerusalem are cut by it. This is the commonest reading, a stone of burden ('even ma'amasah). The Septuagint has 'a trampled stone' for all the nations. The Hebrew verb for 'tear themselves' is a doubled form, 'they will certainly tear' (saroth yissaretu), which stresses the damage.

a: I will hit every horse with terror and its rider with madness
t: The curses of Deuteronomy 28 against the enemy
p: Madness, blindness and terror: Deuteronomy's covenant curses are turned on Jerusalem's attackers.
b: Madness (shiggaon), blindness (ivvaron) and bewilderment (timmahon) are the three plagues of Deuteronomy 28:28: "The LORD will strike you with madness and blindness and a mind in a daze" (Deuteronomy 28:28). In Deuteronomy they are curses on Israel for breaking the covenant. Here the same three fall on the horses and riders of the attackers, and the LORD opens his eyes to Judah. The covenant sanctions that struck Israel now strike the enemies of the restored city. The horse, the chief weapon of the age, has already been taken from Jerusalem (9:10).

a: a fire pot in a stack of wood, a blazing torch in cut grain
t: Fire among the wood and the grain
p: Judah's clan leaders are fire in dry fuel; compare Obadiah 18.
b: The two images are of fire in dry things: a pot of coals set in a stack of wood, a torch in a field of cut grain. They echo Obadiah 18, where the house of Jacob is a fire and the house of Joseph a flame while Esau is stubble. 'Clan leaders' ('alluphim) is a word used of Edom's chiefs (Genesis 36); here it names Judah's heads of clans. The Greek has 'commanders of thousands.' It ends with the city safe 'in its own place, in Jerusalem,' a double mention for emphasis.

a: First the LORD will rescue the tents of Judah
p: Judah's tents (the countryside) are saved before Jerusalem so that David's house and the city will not boast.
b: 'Tents' are the villages and shepherds' camps of Judah, outside Jerusalem. The purpose clause is plain: the LORD saves Judah first 'so that the splendor of David's house and the splendor of the people living in Jerusalem will not be greater than Judah's.' Commentators see a quarrel between the capital and the countryside: the court and the city elite could claim credit for the victory, so the LORD begins with the country people. The same equalizing turn appears in 12:8, where even the one who stumbles will be 'like David.' 'First' (bare'shonah) may also mean 'as at the beginning,' as the Septuagint reads: 'as from the beginning.' 4Q80 preserves the end of this verse.

a: David's house will be like God, like the angel of the LORD at their head
p: David's house is likened to God and then to the angel who led Israel in the exodus.
b: Elohim here is read 'God' or 'a divine being,' and the next phrase softens it: 'like the angel of the LORD going before them.' That angel led Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 14:19; 23:20), and the Hebrew may even call him the LORD's visible presence. The comparison does not call the king divine; it says he will lead the army as God's own messenger. The Septuagint has 'like the house of God.' The Dead Sea scroll 4Q80 (4QXII-e) preserves this verse and reads kelohim, 'like God.' The Christian reading takes David's house as foreshadowing Christ, who is God with his people.

a: a spirit of favor and pleading
p: God pours out a spirit that turns people to repentance and prayer.
b: 'Pour out' (shafakh) is the verb of Isaiah 44:3 (water on the dry ground, my Spirit on your offspring), Ezekiel 39:29 and Joel 2:28. The two nouns, chen and tachanunim, are 'favor' (grace) and 'pleas for favor' (prayers for mercy). The Septuagint has 'a spirit of grace and compassion.' The spirit makes people capable of repentant prayer and grants it. Whether the 'spirit' is the Holy Spirit of Christian teaching, a spirit given by God (a disposition), or the breath of life of 12:1 is a matter of reading. Christians have linked the verse to Pentecost (Acts 2:17) and John 19:37.

a: They will look
p: The pierced one in the New Testament and in the Talmud's Messiah son of Joseph.
b: John 19:37 quotes the line after the soldier's spear: "They will look at the one they pierced" (John 19:37). Revelation 1:7 joins it to Daniel 7:13: 'Every eye will see him, and so will those who pierced him. All the tribes of the earth will mourn over him,' and Matthew 24:30 has the mourning of 'all the tribes of the earth' (the Greek ge can mean 'land' or 'earth,' as the Hebrew 'the land' of 12:12 does). Both John and Revelation use the Greek verb for 'pierce' (ekkentao); the Septuagint does not have it (see the variant). The Talmud (Sukkah 52a) asks why the mourning of 12:12 is so great: for the Messiah son of Joseph who is killed, or for the evil impulse that is slain. See the next note for Jewish readings. Justin Martyr read the passage of the crucified Christ (First Apology 52).

a: the one they pierced through
t: Jewish readings of 'the one they pierced'
p: Targum, Rashi and the Talmud read the verse without a crucified Messiah, and differ among themselves.
b: (1) Targum Jonathan does not translate 'pierced.' It reads: 'they will pray before me because they were exiled' (as Rashi quotes it), so the verb is turned into exile. (2) Rashi takes 'they will look to me' as complaint to God 'about those of them whom the nations thrust through and slew during their exile,' reading the verb as an action of the nations against Israelites, so that 'the one they pierced' is those slain, and 'mourn over it' is mourning over that slaughter. He adds that 'our Sages expounded this in Sukkah 52a as the Messiah son of Joseph, who was slain.' (3) Sukkah 52a asks about the mourning of 12:12 and answers: the Messiah son of Joseph, who is killed, or the evil impulse, which is slain. The grammar is the hinge: if 'et 'asher daqaru is 'the one whom they pierced' and follows 'to me,' as the Plain has it, the LORD himself is the one pierced (the Christian use); if the line is taken as 'to me about those whom they pierced,' the pierced are other people. The Hebrew allows both.

a: as people grieve for an only son
p: The grief is like that of the only child; Isaac, Amos 8:10 and Jeremiah 6:26 use the same picture.
b: The Hebrew is yachid, 'only one': an only child, the whole family's future (Genesis 22:2, Isaac, 'your only one'; Amos 8:10, "the grief over an only son" (Amos 8:10); Jeremiah 6:26). The second line adds a firstborn, who was the heir and the LORD's by right. The Septuagint renders yachid as agapetos, 'beloved' (the word used of Jesus at his baptism: Mark 1:11; Matthew 3:17). Christian readers sometimes link this to the grief at Jesus' death. The Hebrew only says the mourning is the most bitter that families know.

a: Hadad-rimmon
p: A place, a person, a king (Josiah or Ahab) or a god; the verse does not say.
b: Four views. (1) Josiah. He was killed at Megiddo by Pharaoh Neco (2 Kings 23:29; 2 Chronicles 35:22-25), and all Judah and Jeremiah mourned. (2) Two kings. The Aramaic Targum explains the name by two royal deaths, Ahab's (1 Kings 22:34-37) and Josiah's. (3) A place. Jerome knew a village of this name near Jezreel and linked the verse to the mourning for Josiah. (4) A god. Hadad is the West Semitic storm god and Rimmon (Ramman, 'thunderer') his title; he was worshiped in Damascus (2 Kings 5:18). Some scholars read a yearly mourning rite for the dying vegetation god, like that for Tammuz (Ezekiel 8:14). The prophet uses a famous mourning to size Jerusalem's.

a: the clan of Nathan's house by itself
p: Nathan is David's son (Luke 3:31) or Nathan the prophet.
b: The four named groups seem to be four lines of leadership: David's house (kings), Nathan's house, Levi's house (priests), and the Shimeites. Nathan is either David's son through whom Luke 3:31 traces Jesus' line, or the prophet Nathan of 2 Samuel 7 and 12. Each clan mourns 'by itself,' with the women apart, like a family at a funeral. Joel 2:16 shows the opposite: a whole nation gathered, the bridegroom and the bride called out of their rooms.

a: the Shimeites
p: The Shimeites were a Levite clan of Gershon (Numbers 3:21); the Greek reads 'Simeon.'
b: The Shimeites (shim'i) were a clan of Levi through Gershon (Numbers 3:21, 'the clan of the Shimeites'). So the mention follows Levi: first the priestly tribe, then one of its clans, as David's house is followed by a branch (Nathan). The Septuagint reads 'the tribe of Simeon,' the tribe of Jacob's second son; this makes sense of a list of tribes but not of the Hebrew order. The text follows the Hebrew.

a: a spring will be opened
p: A spring from the house of David and Jerusalem; later readers joined it to Ezekiel's river and John's water.
b: A maqor is a spring that wells up from the ground (Jeremiah 2:13 and 17:13 call the LORD 'the spring of living water'). It is 'opened' for the royal house and the city, 'for sin and for impurity,' to cleanse them. Ezekiel 36:25 has the same promise in other words: the LORD sprinkling pure water on his people, and Ezekiel 47:1-12 pictures a river from the Temple. Zechariah 14:8 returns to the water. John joins it to the Feast of Booths and to Jesus: the invitation to the thirsty on the last day (John 7:37-38) and the blood and water from his side (John 19:34, just before the quotation of Zechariah 12:10 in John 19:37). Revelation 22:1 has the river of the water of life.
r: Jeremiah 2:13; Ezekiel 36:25-27; Ezekiel 47:1-12; Zechariah 14:8; John 7:37-38; John 19:34; Revelation 22:1

a: for sin and for impurity
p: Two kinds of fault: moral sin, and ritual impurity.
b: Chatta't is 'sin' (and also the name of the sin offering) and niddah is 'impurity.' The second is the uncleanness of a woman at her monthly separation (Leviticus 12:2; 15:19-20), and by extension any uncleanness that keeps a person from the sanctuary. It could be washed with 'water for impurity' made from the ashes of the red heifer (Numbers 19:9). By using it of Israel's moral state, prophets said the people were unclean as a woman at such a time (Ezekiel 36:17; Lamentations 1:17). Here the spring takes away both what the person has done and the state it left him in. The Septuagint reads the Hebrew as a 'removal and a separation' (metakinesin and chorismon).

a: the spirit of uncleanness
p: The only place the Old Testament has this phrase; the Gospels' 'unclean spirit' uses the same idea.
b: Ruach hattum'ah is 'the spirit of uncleanness,' a force that makes the land unclean, parallel to the idols and the false prophets. It is not a demon in the later sense, but the Gospels' 'unclean spirit' (for example Mark 1:23) uses the same idea of an unclean power at work in a person. The Septuagint has 'the unclean spirit' (to pneuma to akatharton), the Gospels' phrase exactly. The prophets, the idols and the spirit are all driven out together.

a: I will also remove the prophets
p: Does the verse end false prophecy or all prophecy?
b: The verse says 'the prophets' with the article. It sits beside idols and an unclean spirit, and 13:3-6 is about false prophets, so the usual reading is the end of false prophecy under the law of Deuteronomy 13:1-5 and 18:20. Some critical writers hear a late and harsh view of prophecy in the book, perhaps from a time when prophecy had lost its place. Later Jewish teaching said the Holy Spirit left Israel when Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi died (Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 9b), and Christian writers have connected the verse to the fulfillment of prophecy in Christ. Joel 2:28 expects prophesying to spread to all people; the two passages are sometimes set side by side.

a: will pierce him through
p: The parents 'pierce' the false prophet with the verb used for the pierced one in 12:10.
b: Daqar is 'pierce' or 'run through' (Numbers 25:8; Judges 9:54; 1 Samuel 31:4). It is the verb of 12:10 and of this verse alone in the book. The law said a prophet who spoke in the LORD's name what he had not been told, or who spoke for other gods, 'must die' (Deuteronomy 18:20), and that a family member who tried to lure someone from the LORD must not be spared (Deuteronomy 13:6-10). Zechariah pushes the rule to its edge, with mother and father themselves bearing the sentence. It is a picture of a land that has cut off false prophecy at its root, not a rule for later times. Some readers see a deliberate contrast with the pierced one of 12:10. The link exists only in Hebrew: the Septuagint has 'danced in scorn' at 12:10 and, here, that the parents 'will bind his feet' (sympodizo), and in 13:2 it has 'false prophets' for 'the prophets,' so Greek readers saw no connection between the two verses.

a: a cloak of hair
p: A rough hair garment marked a prophet, as with Elijah and John.
b: Elijah was known as 'a hairy man' with a leather loincloth (2 Kings 1:8), and the garment, whether goat or camel hair, stayed the sign of prophets (Elijah's cloak passed to Elisha in 2 Kings 2:13-14). John the Baptist wore camel hair (Matthew 3:4; Mark 1:6). Here the false prophets wear it to look genuine ('to deceive'), and they will drop it in shame. Jesus warns about false prophets who come dressed as sheep (Matthew 7:15), a different disguise with the same lesson.

a: I am no prophet
p: The man's words are those Amos spoke to Amaziah.
b: Amos told the priest Amaziah, "I am no prophet, and I am no prophet's son. I am a herdsman, and I tend sycamore figs" (Amos 7:14). The man here uses the same words, 'I am no prophet,' but for the opposite reason: to deny that he is a prophet at all, to escape the penalty of 13:3. Both are farmers or herdsmen. The echo may show that the writer knew the older prophetic books.

a: What are these wounds between your hands?
p: Cuts on the chest or back, like those of prophets who hurt themselves in ecstasy.
b: 'Between your hands' (bein yadekha) means on the chest, the back or between the arms. The man gives a cover story: 'I was wounded in the house of my friends.' But the reader is meant to see a prophet's self-inflicted wounds. The prophets of Baal on Carmel cut themselves with swords and spears (1 Kings 18:28), and the law forbade such cutting for the dead (Leviticus 19:28; Deuteronomy 14:1). 'My friends' is literally 'my lovers' (me'ahavay); Hosea uses the word for false gods (Hosea 2:7, 10), so a dark pun is possible. The Septuagint has 'my beloved.' The Christian reading of Christ's wounds is a reception, not a translation.

a: against the man who is my partner
p: A rare word: the shepherd is the LORD's close associate, an equal or neighbor.
b: 'Amit occurs elsewhere only in Leviticus (for example 6:2 and 18:20; 19:11, 15, 17), where it means 'fellow, neighbor, associate.' Here it names the shepherd as the LORD's own man, one who stands next to him. The Septuagint has 'a citizen of mine' (andra politen mou), reading the same word as a countryman. Christian readers hear in 'the man next to me' a claim of closeness to God that Jesus fulfills; others read him as a human leader, a good king or ruler. Either way, the LORD calls for the sword against the one beside him.

a: Sword, wake up against my shepherd
p: Jesus quotes it with 'I will strike'; the Hebrew has a command.
b: In Matthew 26:31 Jesus says on the way to the Mount of Olives: "I will strike the shepherd, and the flock's sheep will be scattered" (Matthew 26:31; Mark 14:27 has 'the sheep'). The Hebrew has a command, hak, 'Strike!' addressed to the sword; Matthew and Mark have the first person future, 'I will strike,' which makes God the one who strikes. The Septuagint has the plural, 'Strike the shepherds.' The Hebrew verb for 'scatter' can be 'they will be scattered.' Jesus then says he will go ahead of them to Galilee (Matthew 26:32; Mark 14:28), and in John 16:32 he says the disciples will scatter, each to his own place.
r: Matthew 26:31; Mark 14:27; John 16:32; Zechariah 11:16; Zechariah 10:2; Matthew 26:32

a: I will turn my hand on the little ones
t: 'Turn my hand against': punish or protect?
p: The phrase can mean to strike, or to turn the hand to purify.
b: 'To turn the hand against' (hashiv yad 'al) is mostly hostile. But Isaiah 1:25 uses a similar phrase, 'I will turn my hand against you,' for refining, and that suits the next verses (13:8-9), where the survivors are refined like silver. The 'little ones' (tso'arim) are the small sheep, the least. In Matthew 18:6 and Matthew 18:10-14 Jesus warns about the 'little ones' and says the Father will not lose one. The ambiguity of the Hebrew allows a threat that turns to rescue.
orig: הֲשִׁבֹתִי יָדִי עַל הַצֹּעֲרִים (hashivoti yadi 'al hatso'arim)

a: two parts will be cut off and die, and the third part will be left in it
p: A third survives, as in Ezekiel 5 and Isaiah 6; the survivors are refined.
b: 'Two parts' (literally 'a mouth of two,' as in the double share of Deuteronomy 21:17) fall, and one third is left. Ezekiel 5:2, 12 divides the city's people in three parts: plague and famine, sword, and scattering. In Isaiah 6:13 a tenth is left, and still it is burned. Here the third is brought through fire, and the end is not destruction but a restored bond. The numbers are a pattern, not a count: most of the people are lost, a few remain, and those few are the LORD's people.

a: refine them the way silver is refined
p: Fire purifies the survivors, as silver and gold are refined.
b: Isaiah 48:10 ('I refined you, but not like silver') and Jeremiah 6:27-30 (the prophet as a tester of metals who finds only slag) use the refiner's image, and Malachi 3:2-3 says the Lord will sit as a refiner. Here the aim is that the few survivors come out as pure metal. The result is the covenant formula: the LORD says 'This is my people' and the people answer 'The LORD is my God.' The Hebrew is singular ('he will call'), so the whole remnant is treated as one person. Peter's first letter later uses refined gold for faith tested by trials.

a: I will say, "This is my people,"
p: The old covenant words, reversing 'not my people' in Hosea.
b: 'You will be my people, and I will be your God' sums up the covenant (Exodus 6:7; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:28). Hosea 1:9 had the LORD say 'you are not my people'; Hosea 2:23 reverses it: "I will say to Lo-ammi, 'You are my people,' and he will say, 'My God'" (Hosea 2:23). Zechariah 13:9 repeats Hosea's two lines almost exactly: 'This is my people,' 'The LORD is my God.' So after the sword and the fire the old covenant is renewed. The same formula closes Zechariah 8:8, where the people return to Jerusalem.

a: a day of the LORD is coming
t: The day of the LORD in Zechariah 14
p: A day of battle and of the LORD's kingship; read as past, present or future.
b: The Hebrew is 'a day is coming for the LORD' (yom ba' laYHWH), the day of the LORD, a day that is his to act in (Isaiah 13:6-9; Joel 2:1-2; Amos 5:18-20). Readings: (1) Past. The siege and capture of Jerusalem in 586 BC, or in 63 BC (Pompey), or AD 70, with later hopes added. (2) Present and spiritual. The coming of Christ and the gospel age, in which the nations come to worship (Calvin reads the nations' worship at the feast in 14:16 as the conversion of the nations). (3) Future. A last battle for Jerusalem and the LORD's return to the Mount of Olives (premillennial and dispensational teachers; see the card). (4) Jewish. The chapter is the haftarah for the first day of Booths.
r: Isaiah 13:6-9; Joel 2:1-2; Joel 3:1-16; Amos 5:18-20; Ezekiel 38:1-39:20; Zephaniah 1:14-18

a: as on the day he fought in battle
t: The LORD fights as at the Exodus
p: The war of the LORD against the nations repeats his old victories.
b: The picture is of the LORD as warrior, with Moses' words after the sea (Exodus 15:3, 'The LORD is a man of war'), and Joshua's day when 'the LORD fought for Israel' (Joshua 10:14). 'As when he fights on a day of battle' recalls those. The earlier prophets repeat it: Isaiah 63:1-6; Habakkuk 3. Here the LORD himself goes out, not an army, and the victory comes with the splitting of the mountain and a plague (14:12-15). Joel 3:9-16 gives the same war at 'the Valley of Jehoshaphat.'
r: Exodus 14:14; Exodus 15:3; Joshua 10:14; Isaiah 63:1-6; Habakkuk 3:3-15; Joel 3:9-16

a: His feet will stand, on that day, on the Mount of Olives
p: The ridge east of Jerusalem; the glory of the LORD left toward it and will return from it.
b: The Mount of Olives is the ridge east of Jerusalem across the Kidron valley. This is the only place the Hebrew Bible calls it 'the mountain of the Olives'; 2 Samuel 15:30 has 'the slope of the Olives,' where David wept as he fled. Ezekiel saw the glory of the LORD leave the city and stand on 'the mountain east of the city' (Ezekiel 11:23) and return from the east (Ezekiel 43:2). In the Gospels Jesus teaches on it (Matthew 24:3), prays near it (Matthew 26:30), and rides down it (Luke 19:37). At the ascension two men say Jesus 'will come this same way' (Acts 1:11), and Acts 1:12 places the ascent at the Mount of Olives. Josephus reports that under the governor Felix a prophet from Egypt led a crowd to the mount and promised that Jerusalem's walls would fall (Antiquities 20.8.6).
r: 2 Samuel 15:30; Ezekiel 11:23; Ezekiel 43:2; Matthew 24:3; Luke 19:37; Acts 1:11-12

a: for the valley between the mountains will reach to Azal
t: The valley of my mountains and Azal
p: A hard verse: an escape route through the new valley, or a valley that is blocked.
b: The new valley made by the splitting mountain (14:4) is an escape route. The Hebrew says 'the valley of my mountains' and then 'the valley of mountains will reach to Azal.' Azal is not found elsewhere and the place is unknown, perhaps near the Olives; the Septuagint reads 'Jasod' (Iasod). The old versions read the verb differently: the Hebrew (and so the Plain) has nastem, 'you will flee,' while the Septuagint reads 'the valley will be blocked' (Swete's text), which suggests a different pointing of the same consonants. See the variant.

a: the earthquake in the time of King Uzziah of Judah
p: Amos 1:1 dates his words by the same quake; Josephus ties it to Uzziah's sin.
b: Amos 1:1 dates the prophet's words 'two years before the earthquake,' in the reign of Uzziah (about 790-740 BC). Excavators at Hazor and other sites have reported damage from a quake in the mid-8th century BC, but the dating is debated. Zechariah's phrase shows that the quake was remembered 250 years later. Josephus connects it with Uzziah's attempt to burn incense in the Temple, when, he says, the Temple was split and the sun's rays fell on the king's face (Antiquities 9.10.4). That is a later tradition and is not in 2 Chronicles 26. The quake serves here as a measure of what is coming.

a: all the holy ones
p: Probably angels coming with the LORD as his army; the Hebrew says 'holy ones.'
b: 'Holy ones' (qedoshim) are God's heavenly court and army: Deuteronomy 33:2 ('myriads of holy ones'), Psalm 89:5-7, Daniel 7:18. Jude 14 quotes 1 Enoch for the same coming: 'The Lord has come with his holy ones by the tens of thousands' (Jude 14). Paul uses the same phrase of the Lord's return (1 Thessalonians 3:13), and the church has read it as angels, or the saints with him, or both. The Plain keeps 'holy ones' without choosing. The Hebrew 'with you' is addressed to the prophet or the people (see the variant).

a: at the hour of evening, there will be light
p: The darkest day ends in light; Isaiah 60 and Revelation 21-22 share the picture.
b: The strange 'one day' of 14:6-7 has no normal day or night, and then, at the time of evening when light should fade, there is light. Isaiah 60:19-20 says the sun and moon will be replaced by the LORD as an everlasting light, and Revelation takes this up for the new Jerusalem: no night there, no lamp or sun needed (Revelation 21:23-25; 22:5). Zechariah is the older text. The turn (light at evening) is a reversal of the evening that closes the prophet's world.

a: living waters will go out of Jerusalem
p: A river from Jerusalem to both seas; compare Ezekiel 47, Joel 3:18, Psalm 46 and John 7.
b: 'Living water' is running water, as in a spring (Jeremiah 2:13). Water from the city that has no big river is a miracle (Psalm 46:4, 'A river! Its channels gladden the city of God'). Ezekiel 47:1-12 sees a stream from the Temple that heals the Dead Sea, and Joel 3:18 says 'A spring will flow out from the house of the LORD.' Genesis 2:10 has the river of Eden. Half goes to the 'eastern sea' (the Dead Sea) and half to the 'western sea' (the Mediterranean), in summer and winter, in the dry season when streams fail. John 7 sets Jesus' cry at the last day of Booths, when a water ceremony was held (Mishnah Sukkah 4:9-10; 5:1): "If anyone is thirsty, he should come to me and drink" (John 7:37). Revelation 22:1-2 has the river from the throne.
r: Ezekiel 47:1-12; Joel 3:18; Psalm 46:4; Genesis 2:10; John 7:37-38; Revelation 22:1-2

a: the LORD will be one, and his name will be one
p: Echoes the Shema; the Aleinu prayer ends with this verse.
b: The verse takes the Shema, "The LORD is our God. The LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4), and says that on that day the world will see it. The LORD will not be one among many gods; he will be the only one, with one name, 'king over the whole earth.' In Jewish worship the Aleinu prayer quotes this verse. Its point is the end of the nations' many gods (see 13:2) and of the many names they used for them. Christian readers have often heard the hope of one name in Christ's name above every name.

a: from Geba down to Rimmon
t: From Geba to Rimmon, and the gates
p: From Judah's northern to its southern limit; then the city's gates and towers.
b: Geba was at the northern edge of Judah (2 Kings 23:8 says 'from Geba to Beersheba'), and Rimmon is in the Negev (Joshua 15:32). The whole land becomes a flat plain like the Arabah, the rift valley, and only Jerusalem stands raised. The gates and towers fix its limits: the Benjamin Gate (north), the First Gate and the Corner Gate (northwest), the Tower of Hananel (Jeremiah 31:38; Nehemiah 3:1) and the king's winepresses (southeast). These are names from the pre-exilic city and from Nehemiah's rebuilt wall, which suits the Persian-period date and the earlier setting alike. 'Rise high' translates a rare form (ra'amah) that most take as 'rise' or 'be lifted up'; the Septuagint reads it as the place name Ramah (Rama), 'Ramah will stay in its place.'

a: put under the ban
p: The ban meant destruction; the last curse of Joshua and Deuteronomy ends.
b: Cherem is the 'ban,' the dedication of a city or people to destruction (Joshua 6:17; Deuteronomy 7:2; 20:17). A city under the ban was left in ruins. The Septuagint renders it anathema (curse), the word Revelation 22:3 echoes: 'Nothing will be under a curse any longer.' Zechariah says Jerusalem will never again be so condemned, in contrast to the cities Joshua destroyed and to Jerusalem's own fall. The book of the Twelve ends on the same word, but with the threat that the LORD will strike the land with a ban if hearts are not turned (the last verse of Malachi).

a: Judah will also be fighting at Jerusalem
p: The little Hebrew preposition be can mean at, in or against.
b: The Hebrew is tillachem biYerushalaim. The preposition be usually means 'in' or 'at' (Judah fights in the city's defense), but it can mean 'against' (Judah forced to fight on the enemy's side, as 12:2 hints). The Septuagint has 'in Jerusalem.' The context after 14:13 fits a Judah that joins the fight. The wealth of the nations being gathered is the reversal of 14:1, where Jerusalem's own loot was divided.

a: keep the Feast of Booths
p: The harvest feast, the festival of rain and of the LORD as king.
b: Booths (Sukkot) is the autumn feast of ingathering when the people lived in leafy shelters (Leviticus 23:34, 42-43; Deuteronomy 16:13-15). Solomon dedicated the Temple at it (1 Kings 8:2), and Ezra's people kept it (Ezra 3:4) and Nehemiah's (Nehemiah 8:14-17). It is the time when the winter rain is prayed for, and so fits 14:17-18, where the nations that stay away get no rain (Mishnah Taanit 1:1 on when rain is first mentioned). In the Talmud seventy bulls were offered at it for the seventy nations of the world (Sukkah 55b). Zechariah 14 is the haftarah for its first day. John 7-8 sets Jesus' teaching at this feast, with its water and its lights.
r: Leviticus 23:34; Deuteronomy 16:13; Nehemiah 8:14-17; Ezra 3:4; John 7:2; John 7:37-38

a: If the clan of Egypt does not go up or come
p: Egypt has the Nile, so the 'no rain' line is odd for it; the plague is the threat that matters.
b: Egypt is named because it is the land of the Nile, not the rain. Deuteronomy 11:10 says it was watered 'with your foot' by irrigation, unlike Canaan, which depends on rain. So a threat of no rain would have little force against Egypt. That is a real puzzle in the Hebrew, which says only 'and not on them' (the Plain supplies 'rain' from 14:17). Some read the words as irony or as a leftover from 14:17, and the Septuagint leaves them out; either way, the weight of the verse is on the plague, which is the penalty that does reach Egypt. Egypt is also the old oppressor, and the plagues of Exodus fell on it. But Isaiah 19:19-25 foresees Egypt serving the LORD with an altar and sacrifice, blessed as 'my people Egypt.' The oracle thus sets Egypt in the shape of the nations: first enemy, then worshiper, with the penalty for those who will not come.

a: Holy to the LORD
t: 'Holy to the LORD' on the horses' bells
p: The inscription of the high priest's gold plate is moved to a horse's bell.
b: "Holy to the LORD" was engraved on the gold plate on the high priest's forehead (Exodus 28:36; 39:30). Now it is written on the bells of the war horses, the animals the prophet hates (9:10; 10:5; 12:4), and the common cooking pots in the Temple will be like the holy bowls of the altar. The word translated 'bells' (metsillot) is found only here and may be 'bells' or 'bridles' (so the Septuagint, chalinon). The whole city, Judah, the pots of every household become fit for sacrifice. Holiness reaches into daily things.

a: the house of the LORD of Armies
p: The last verse of the book may be the Temple cleansed of traders; the Gospels' Temple scene echoes it.
b: The last words say that no 'Canaanite' will be in the Temple. The old nation of the Canaanites is gone, so the word means a trader or merchant (see the variant). The Gospels show Jesus driving out sellers and money-changers from the temple: John 2:14-16 ('Stop turning my Father's house into a house for trading') uses a nearly identical picture, and Matthew 21:12-13 and Mark 11:15-17 add Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11. Many Christian readers have seen Zechariah 14:21 in the background of the scene, as a prophecy of a Temple made pure; some commentators think the evangelists do not draw on it directly.
r: John 2:14-16; Matthew 21:12-13; Mark 11:15-17; Isaiah 56:7; Jeremiah 7:11; Zephaniah 1:11
